name: SedonaDB (Apache Sedona DB)
baseline: GeoPandas 1.1.1 and DuckDB 1.4.0 (SpatialBench single-node comparison); neither is one of the listed C++ baselines
workload: SpatialBench queries 1-12 (spatial analytics SQL/DataFrame queries) at scale factors 1 and 10, single node, run time in seconds.
claimed_speedup: README states no ratio in text; the two bar charts are the evidence. Labelled values read from the charts: SF1 q7 GeoPandas 137.0 s (SedonaDB bar is about 1 s, bar reading); SF1 q9 SedonaDB 0.23 s vs GeoPandas 0.28 s while the DuckDB bar is about 50 s (unlabelled, bar reading); SF1 q10 DuckDB 207.8 s vs SedonaDB about 19 s and GeoPandas about 46 s (bar readings). SF10 q9 SedonaDB 0.38 s, GeoPandas 0.48 s, DuckDB 943.0 s; SF10 q11 SedonaDB 97.5 s and q12 145.7 s where DuckDB and GeoPandas show error or timeout. Against DuckDB the result is mixed: SedonaDB is clearly slower on q5 at both scales (about 4.8 s vs 1.3 s at SF1, about 51 s vs 14.5 s at SF10, bar readings) and roughly equal or modestly faster on most other queries.
tradeoffs: Rust engine with Python (PyPI apache-sedona[db]), SQL and R APIs, not a C++ library; it is a spatial DataFrame/SQL analytics engine rather than a geometry kernel or index, so it does not replace Boost.Geometry, CGAL or GEOS inside C++ code. Version 0.1.0 benchmarked, an early release.
caveats: First-party (Apache Sedona project) numbers shown only as images in the README; the full results page (sedona.apache.org/spatialbench) is blocked from this environment (EGRESS_BLOCKED), so hardware, settings and timeouts could not be read. Baselines are other spatial stacks (GeoPandas, DuckDB), not GEOS/CGAL/Boost.Geometry directly; that GeoPandas and DuckDB spatial sit on GEOS is general knowledge, not stated on the page. The benchmark suite (SpatialBench) is by the same project. Mixed against DuckDB (slower on q5). The chart also shows DuckDB and GeoPandas failing or timing out on several SF10 queries, so those 'wins' are not speed ratios. Bar readings are approximate.

name: Flatbush
baseline: RBush (dynamic JavaScript R-tree; counts as an R-tree baseline)
workload: Static packed Hilbert R-tree over 1,000,000 random rectangles: index build plus bounding-box and k-nearest-neighbour searches (README table is Flatbush-only).
claimed_speedup: README says Flatbush is similar to RBush with 'Faster indexing and search, with much lower memory footprint'; no RBush timings or ratio appear on the page. Flatbush-only numbers: index 1,000,000 rectangles 109ms; 1000 searches 1% area 66ms; 10000 searches of 1 neighbor 30ms; 1 search of 1,000,000 neighbors 84ms.
tradeoffs: Static index: no add or remove after finish(). The whole index is one ArrayBuffer (transferable between threads, storable as a compact binary file). JavaScript only; the README lists ports for C++, Rust, C# and Python (a C++ port exists as chusitoo/flatbush) and a Rust port with ABI compatibility (geo-index, already catalogued).
caveats: The speed-up over RBush is a qualitative README claim: the benchmark table has only a flatbush column and bench.js in the repo does not import RBush, so the comparison cannot be reproduced from the repo. Not C++ and not compared with Boost.Geometry or CGAL. Kept as the single tier D entry of this run because of notability.

name: earcut.hpp
baseline: earcut.js (the original JavaScript implementation); the README also names CGAL and libtess2 as slower but gives no numbers for them
workload: Triangulating 119,680 real-world polygons (1.9M vertices) cut from Mapbox Vector Tile windows at zooms 4-16, whole set timed.
claimed_speedup: README: ~276 ms for the whole 119,680-polygon set on a MacBook Pro M1 Pro (2021), 'noticeably faster than the JS original' (no JS timing or ratio on the page); optional Delaunay refinement adds ~98 ms.
tradeoffs: Header-only C++14 polygon triangulator (ear slicing with z-order curve and spatial hashing). Trades quality and guaranteed correctness for speed: assumes valid polygons, output is not conforming (T-junctions) and not Delaunay unless the opt-in mapbox::refine pass is used (that pass uses non-robust predicates). README points to CGAL or libtess2 when correctness on bad input is needed.
caveats: The only baseline with a stated relation is the JS original and no baseline number is on the page; the README's 'slower and larger' remark about CGAL and libtess2 is qualitative. test/bench.cpp does include a libtess2 comparison benchmark (comparison/libtess2.hpp, Google Benchmark, CMake default build type Release) but its results are not published, so a verifier would need to run it. Compiler and flags for the 276 ms figure are not stated. The speedup over a same-algorithm JS port is a weak result.

name: delaunator-cpp
baseline: mapbox/delaunator (JavaScript original); no CGAL or Triangle comparison in the repo
workload: 2D Delaunay triangulation of uniform random points (2,000 to 1,000,000) and 45K GeoJSON nodes.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Probably the fastest C++ open source 2D Delaunay implementation' and '~10% faster than JS version for 1M uniform points'. Own timings: 45K geojson nodes 22 ms; 100,000 uniform points 63 ms; 1,000,000 uniform points 994 ms. PR #8 shows an earlier '6 times faster than JS' claim was challenged by the JS author and corrected to ~20-30%, then ~10%.
hardware: 4 X 2300 MHz CPU (model not stated), run dated 2018-09-29
tradeoffs: 2D unconstrained Delaunay only; plain std::vector<double> coordinate input (x0,y0,x1,y1,...); header-style port of the JS algorithm, not robust-predicate based.
caveats: Baseline is the JS version of the same algorithm, not a C++ incumbent such as CGAL, Triangle or Boost.Geometry. Numbers are first-party from 2018 with no compiler or flags and no CPU model. The 'fastest C++' wording is hedged ('Probably'). A WebSearch summary of the HN thread 'Exact, parallel 2D Delaunay triangulation for int32 coordinates' (item 49125532, not opened) lists delaunator-cpp at roughly the same runtime as Triangle (about 11x a Delaunay32 baseline) and about 3.7x slower than Delaunay32 at 1M points, so it is not shown to beat Triangle. Delaunay32 is already catalogued.
